title: Monthly report from three exports that disagree
prompt:
Oakline Pet Supply's founder wants the May 2026 marketing report and has noticed that the ad platforms, the analytics tool and the order system each tell a different story. You are supplied three exports: weekly figures from the ad platforms, purchase events from the analytics tool, and the order system. Every figure you cite must come from them.

Use these definitions exactly:
- The order system is the record of what was sold. A real order has an `order_date` in May 2026 and a `status` other than cancelled or test.
- Net revenue = `gross_usd` minus `refund_usd`, summed over real orders.
- Ad spend = total `spend_usd` in the ad platform export.
- Blended ROAS = net revenue ÷ ad spend.
- A duplicate analytics row is any purchase row beyond the first for the same `order_id`.

Write the report: an executive summary of no more than 150 words that leads with the month's real results; then why the three sources disagree, with the size of each difference; then what to fix so that next month's numbers agree. Show enough method that a colleague could re-derive each headline figure.

End the report with an answer block in exactly this format, one line per answer, each line starting with the label:

A1: <ad spend, in dollars>
A2: <number of real orders>
A3: <net revenue, in dollars>
A4: <number of duplicate analytics rows>
A5: <blended ROAS, to two decimals>
A6: <total conversions the ad platforms report, all platforms combined>

This is an internal report. Fetch nothing external and do not invent benchmarks.

completion.check: The response ends with the required answer block and all 6 labeled answers A1-A6 are present and parseable.
A1 states total ad spend; full credit within 0.5%, zero credit beyond 10% off.
A2 states the number of real orders as defined; full credit for the exact count, zero credit eight or more off.
A3 states net revenue as defined; full credit within 0.5%, zero credit beyond 5% off.
A4 states the number of duplicate analytics rows as defined; full credit for the exact count, zero credit eight or more off.
A5 states blended ROAS as defined; full credit within 1%, zero credit beyond 10% off.
A6 states the conversions the ad platforms report, all platforms combined; full credit for the exact count, zero credit thirty or more off.
The report opens with an executive summary of about 150 words or fewer, placed before any table or method.

skill_adherence.check: The executive summary's headline results are the reconciled figures (real orders, net revenue, ad spend, blended ROAS), not analytics revenue or platform-reported revenue.
The platforms' combined reported conversions are never presented as the number of orders the business received, and platform-reported revenue is never presented as the month's revenue.

The report explains the differences between the sources with their sizes: the duplicate analytics rows, the orders excluded as cancelled or test, the refunds deducted, the orders dated outside May, and the gap between platform-reported conversions and real orders. At least four of these five are given with a number.
Every figure presented as a result is derivable from the three exports under the stated definitions. No benchmark, forecast, margin or customer figure is stated as if it were data.

best_practices.check: The fixes address the causes found: stop the purchase event firing more than once per order or deduplicate it by order id; keep test orders out of reporting; bring refunds and cancellations into the revenue figure; and label platform conversions as platform-reported. At least three of these four are present.
For each headline figure the report says which rows were included and which were excluded, so the figure can be re-derived.
The executive summary can be understood by a founder in one reading: it states the month's orders, net revenue, ad spend and return in plain words, without unexplained abbreviations.
